newsitem.title: USA: New York holds 236th St. Patrick's parade.
newsitem.headline: New York holds 236th St. Patrick's parade.

text.p: Enthusiastic crowds sporting Irish-inspired garb from green socks to green hats to green hair lined the sidewalks of Fifth Avenue on Monday to watch and celebrate the 236th annual St. Patrick's Day parade.
Onlookers wore emerald bowties, waved Irish flags and carried babies with shamrock-shaped bibs as they cheered the estimated 200,000 marchers.

The day honouring the Irish began with a traditional mass at St. Patrick's Cathedral led by Roman Catholic Cardinal John O'Connor. He urged generosity toward immigrants and the poor, in whom he said one could see "the faces and the voices of our ancestors."

Before joining the parade up Fifth Avenue, which was decorated with a green line up the centre, Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, in a shiny green tie, officiated at a wedding at Gracie Mansion, the mayor's residence.

The bride was Davina Ismail-Massey, a London woman who contacted a New York City radio station in January saying she was having trouble arranging a March wedding at City Hall. Giuliani offered to marry Ismail-Massey and Tyrone Giblin at a St. Patrick's Day breakfast.
The traditional parade featured seemingly endless waves of uniformed police, firefighters, marching bands, baton twirlers and bagpipe players.
One firefighter name Curly Bohan got extra applause for the shamrock he shaved into the the back of his head.
An unofficial participant, a marathon runner named Eileen Sheehan, opted to run the length of the parade route, pausing to dance jigs when the procession would pause.
"New York is the best place to be Irish and the best place to run, so I just thought I would hop in," she said.
Vendor Jerry Montanio travelled across the country from Salt Lake City in hopes of selling a load of 900 floppy green top hats for $10 apiece.
"If I sell them all, I'll be lucky like the Irish," he said.
As the parade wound down, many onlookers headed for the hundreds of Irish bars for whom St. Patrick's Day is the busiest day of the year.
More than a million onlookers were expected at the parade, but police did not have an official crowd estimate available.

A dispute erupted among about 30 youths a block away from the parade route that left an 18-year-old man critically injured and on a respirator at a local hospital, police said. A second man was less seriously injured, and a third man, suspected of being the assailant, was being sought, police said. There were no arrests.
The parade also had its sombre side, including a moment of silence in remembrance of the 150th anniversary of the Irish famine.
Missing from the election-year parade were three Democrats seeking to challenge the Republican mayor in November.

Manhattan Borough President Ruth Messinger, Bronx Borough President Fernando Ferrer and the Rev. Al Sharpton all said they would not join the parade because its organisers, a Roman Catholic group called the Ancient Order of Hibernians, have refused to let a gay and lesbian group march.
Giuliani, who marches each year, said: "This is a parade about Irish pride, and June is the Gay and Lesbian Pride parade. They'll have a chance to demonstrate their pride."

Members of the group, the Irish Lesbian and Gay Organisation, held a protest on Fifth Avenue before the parade began. Thirty-five people were arrested on charges of disorderly conduct or resisting arrest.
